newsitem.title: USA: Intel countersues Digital, claiming patent infringement.
newsitem.headline: Intel countersues Digital, claiming patent infringement.

text.p: In an escalation of a legal battle between two computer giants, Intel Corp. filed a countersuit against Digital Equipment Corp. on Tuesday, claiming infringement on 14 patents.

Intel's counterclaim, filed in U.S. District Court in Worcester, Mass., comes three months after Digital surprised the industry with its lawsuit alleging Intel had stolen key elements of patented technology for the design of its popular Pentium processors.

"From a legal standpoint, we needed to maintain a more level playing field," Intel spokesman Chuck Mulloy said of the countersuit. "That is the intent here, to defend ourselves. this is a defensive posture."

Intel's countersuit claims that Digital infringed patents covering microprocessor architecture and design, semiconductor manufacturing, video encoding/decoding, thermal management for laptop computers and other areas.
"These are not frivolous patents," Intel spokesman Chuck Malloy said. Nevertheless, he said the counterclaim was only necessary since Digital sued Intel.
Analysts said Intel's counterclaim gives the Santa Clara, Calif. microprocessor maker some leverage and will likely lead to an out-of-court settlement.
"I think this enhances the likelihood of a negotiated settlement. I think Intel wanted a little leverage here," said William Milton, an analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman.
The patent squabble has had little impact on the two companies operations, but could become a distraction if a full-blown court battle ensued, analysts said.
"Court battles are expensive, the outcome is often unpredictable, they are time consuming. Even if one side wins, the case can be appealed," Milton said.

Intel and Maynard, Mass.-based Digital have reportedly held talks in an attempt to reach an out-of-court settlement, but an Intel spokesman declined to comment on whether the two companies have held any recent negotiations.
Digital did not immediately return phone calls seeking comment.
"Whether Intel is firing blanks or nuclear warheads remains to be seen," said Terry Shannon, editor of the independent newsletter "Shannon Knows DEC."
"I think that makes it more likely that's there's going to be some sort of settlement," Shannon said.

Charles Rule, an antitrust lawyer and former head of the antitrust division at the Department of Justice, said civil suits most often end in settlements. Patent suits are sometimes settled through cross-licensing deals with limited royalty agreements, he said.

"It's not unusual to see those kind of counterclaims filed," he said. "It is somehwhat rare, although patents are somewhat different, that you litigate civil claims. So it would not be surprising if they resolved them here."
